Tafelberg School Property

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tafelberg, a blue print for cape town and south Africa

Summary:
This is a story of a school that was sold by the Western Cape Government to an organisation without due public process. It raised the ire of organisations because this was the perfect opportunity for local and provincial govt to, in terms of SPLUMA, to redress the imbalances of the past and create affordable housing in the city centre. Something which, contrary to the constitution, the western cape has failed to do since the dawn of democracy. This is the story of how a local NGO got the high court to halt the sale and order a public participation process. At this stage, according to a petition it’s split 50/50, those sea point residents opposed to and for it. We do hone in on a property mogul Seeff properties who took it upon himself to get a petition going not to support the development of this area for affordable housing, and he even took it upon himself to tell the Jewish community not to attend the public process meetings.

We hear exactly why adorable housing should be considered in this area of city. One care giver, who was a domestic worker, and who has lived in domestic quarters will describe how and why she should be allowed the opportunity to stay in affordable housing in sea point. She says that people are scared that it will bring the value of properties down in the area but she says "why is it that I downgrade your property if I don’t downgrade your children when you go to work?"





Further information:
In the meantime the public works dept has now issued a report suggesting that affordable housing can be developed in sea point if it is cross subsidized by commercial retail outlets and we will hear from the head of Malcolm McCarthy who heads up the national association of social housing who has travelled extensively overseas and seen how affordable housing can be achieved in cities. We also then show just how the city needs to get its properties right for in the gentrification of the city, some families are being evicted to the landscapes of the cape flats, similar to the evictions which took place during the apartheid era. We will quiz both the city and the province to show us exactly the land that they have which is not being used and which could be used for affordable housing.

• Does katz not have an upsound where he expresses his views about affordable housing, does he support or reject the concept/ We need to know this from him. In the interest of balance we need to clarify his position as well so that he doesn’t look like the bad guy – when he isn’t???

Press Release:


Sea Point Housing
Despite one of its own departments earmarking the site for affordable housing in Sea Point to help redress some of the injustices of apartheid era planning, the Western Cape government went ahead and sold the Tafelberg School property to the highest bidder. However, the sale was halted on a technicality when the law centre, Ndifuna Ukwazi, took the provincial government to court. A new process was ordered and this time there were over 8 000 submissions to the provincial government for and against affordable housing on the site. Carte Blanche takes a look at this divided community.


Script:


TAFELBERG SCHOOL (SEA POINT HOUSING) SCRIPT

76-year-old Mrs. Brenda Smith grew up in this house in Salt River on the fringe of the Cape Town CBD. She and her family have rented this property all their lives. Salt River is their home.

Mrs. Smith: It’s close to the shops hospitals and schools.

Gentrification of the area has meant that several homes in Bromwell street including Mrs. Smiths, have been sold by landlords to private developers. By law, the evicted families have to be provided alternative housing. Many could be relocated to a settlement 30km from the city called Wolwerivier.

Sarita: We have people who do not have the option of affordable housing in the inner city who are being pushed out because there is no option. Private rents are way too expensive.

Sarita Pillay is a researcher at Ndifuna Ukwazi, a legal clinic, which provides legal and organizational support to the Reclaim the City campaign. It’s fighting for the development of affordable housing in the CBD and immediate surrounds.
Sarita: There hasn’t been any affordable rental housing built by the city within inner city cape town in the post apartheid period.

Reclaim the city has earmarked several sites in the cbd and it surrounds. One of those is the Tafelberg school, a 2 hectare provincial owned property right in the center of Sea Point. Rentals here have sky rocketed in recent years. Expect to fork at least R10 000 a month for a bachelor flat. Reclaim the city believes that an affordable housing complex here would start addressing segregation caused by apartheid spatial planning.

LINK: THIS PROPERTY IN SEA POINT, WHICH UNTIL 2010 WAS A REMEDIAL SCHOOL, CAN WELL BECOME A BLUE PRINT FOR HOW VACANT PROPERTY OWNED BY NATIONAL, PROVINCIAL AND LOCAL GOVENRMENTS ARE USED TO PROVIDE AFFORDABLE HOUSING. BUT ITS NOT WITHOUT CONTROVERSY.

Affordable housing estates are state subsidized rental accommodation for low income earners, and are managed by a social housing organization. The mere thought of affordable housing in their midst has raised the hackles of many Sea Point residents - judging from social media postings. A common concern is that the area could be downgraded. This attitude upsets Elizabeth Gqoboka, a spokesperson for Reclaim the city, and a care giver who has lived in Sea Point for many years in a tiny room behind a block of flats.

Elizabeth: If you have a domestic worker particularly and a caregiver that is caring for your health. Someone that is taking care of your household, raising your children, why can’t these people be good enough to live with you.

Life long resident, Allan’s Hirsch agrees. He told us that in 1936 his father fled Nazi Germany and settled in Sea Point. Hirsch, now a professor at UCT, said that during his childhood he and his family were able to benefit from living in rent controlled accommodation,

John: It does show you though how important a leg up is to give you the required momentum?
Allan: I think so. And I think that the kind of people who would occupy these apartments are people who have jobs and have children and would be able to use that advantage very effectively.

That thinking seems to have initially been shared by the western cape dept.’s of human settlement who expressed interest in this site for affordable housing in 2013. However, the department of transport and public works sold it privately for R135 000 000 in 2015. The dept. declined an interview saying it would be inappropriate to comment at this stage.

Lance Katz is the vice chairperson of the Phyllis Jowell Jewish, day school which bought the property.

Lance Katz: Province put the property up for sale. We tendered for it, followed due process and we were awarded the bid based on the rules of the tender.

But when Ndifuna ukwazi and Reclaim the City got wind that the site was (being) sold off privately, they took the Western Cape Government to court. They argued that in terms of the government act, GIAMA, state, provincial and local government can only sell a property if it declared “surplus”, meaning it no longer supports service delivery objectives. - Like housing.

Mandisa: In order to understand that, we need to understand the need for housing, the extent of the housing backlog currently is almost half a million in Cape Town.

The court also heard that The sale of the property was not advertised in the provinces’ three official languages

John: So it was halted on a technicality but a very important technicality?
Mandisa: So where it was only published in English and Afrikaans, there is also specific requirement that it also be published in IsiXhosa. Now that that wasn’t done is also telling of the type of stereotype in terms of who can and can’t have a say on how public land is used.

A judge halted the sale, and ordered that the process start over. This time there were over 8000 submissions, both for and against the sale. The Western Cape Government then produced a financial feasibility study for 270 affordable housing units on the site.
That study was debated at a public participation meeting in January. Sea Point residents also heard about the plight of domestic workers who were being evicted from the suburb – like Siphokazi Madikane who says she now has to spend a quarter of her salary on transport to and from Langa township, outside the city. But She was raised in Sea Point and lived there in rented domestic quarters until last year when she was evicted and could not find any other accommodation she could afford.

Siphokazi: It was sad for me to leave Sea Point because that is where I grew up. That is where my life is. That is where I feel like I am protected.

She and her two children now live in this room costing R1600 per month. She could afford, and would be an ideal tenant for the affordable housing scheme proposed by Ndifuna Ukwazi and a social housing organizations called Nasho

LINK: There are some very strong opinions on both sides of the tafelberg debate but there also appears to be a misconception around what exactly affordable housing is.

It’s well constructed accommodation that blends into the environment. The strength of the scenario submitted by Ndifuna Uwazi is that 121 sectional title units will cross subsidize the building of 316 rental units, as well as actually pay for the land. Malcolm McCarthy who worked on the submission and who heads up NASHO has travelled extensively overseas and studied successful affordable housing schemes in major cities, which he says can be replicated in cape town.

Malcolm: It provides enormous potential for the city to actually show that it is possible to have well integrated residential accommodation.

And that’s already on the cards. This last week saw the release to the public of 6 proposals for the redevelopment of the foreshore precinct. City of cape town mayco member. Brett heron says that affordable housing in the cbd is now a priority.

Brett Heron: So we are planning to address the location of public housing head on in this term of office and we have restructured our administration in order to drive that agenda.

The city made it a pre requisite that each proposal make provision for affordable housing. One submission included 4000 such units.


It would be a dream come true if Siphokazi and her children could move back to the CBD, either to the fore shore precinct or sea point. A decision over the tafelberg school by the w3atern cape government is immanent. Lance Katz who supports the concept of affordable housing, says that he will accept the decision by province.


Lane Katz: Province ultimately still need to decide whether they are going to uphold the sale or not. I actually think the process that has come out of that in terms of a public debate around the issue has actually been helpful.

The decision over tafeberg could be ground breaking.

Mandisa: IT might be about doing what might be seemingly unpopular but I think that’s what transformation and an inclusive city requires.

A judge halted the sale, and ordered that the process start over. This time there were over 8000 submissions, both for and against the sale. The Western Cape Government then produced a financial feasibility study for 270 affordable housing units on the site. That study was debated at a public participation meeting in January. Sea Point residents also heard about the plight of domestic workers who were being evicted from the suburb – like Siphokazi Madikane who says she now has to spend a quarter of her salary on transport to and from Langa township, outside the city. But She was raised in Sea Point and lived there in rented domestic quarters until last year when she was evicted and could not find any other accommodation she could afford. Siphokazi: It was sad for me to leave Sea Point because that is where I grew up. That is where my life is. That is where I feel like I am protected. She and her two children now live in this room costing R1600 per month. She could afford, and would be an ideal tenant for the affordable housing scheme proposed by Ndifuna Ukwazi and a social housing organizations called Nasho LINK: There are some very strong opinions on both sides of the tafelberg debate but there also appears to be a misconception around what exactly affordable housing is. It’s well constructed accommodation that blends into the environment. The strength of the scenario submitted by Ndifuna Uwazi is that 121 sectional title units will cross subsidize the building of 316 rental units, as well as actually pay for the land. Malcolm McCarthy who worked on the submission and who heads up NASHO has travelled extensively overseas and studied successful affordable housing schemes in major cities, which he says can be replicated in cape town. Malcolm: It provides enormous potential for the city to actually show that it is possible to have well integrated residential accommodation. And that’s already on the cards. This last week saw the release to the public of 6 proposals for the redevelopment of the foreshore precinct. City of cape town mayco member. Brett heron says that affordable housing in the cbd is now a priority. Brett Heron: So we are planning to address the location of public housing head on in this term of office and we have restructured our administration in order to drive that agenda. The city made it a pre requisite that each proposal make provision for affordable housing. One submission included 4000 such units. It would be a dream come true if Siphokazi and her children could move back to the CBD, either to the fore shore precinct or sea point. A decision over the tafelberg school by the w3atern cape government is immanent. Lance Katz who supports the concept of affordable housing, says that he will accept the decision by province. Lane Katz: Province ultimately still need to decide whether they are going to uphold the sale or not. I actually think the process that has come out of that in terms of a public debate around the issue has actually been helpful. The decision over tafeberg could be ground breaking. Mandisa: IT might be about doing what might be seemingly unpopular but I think that’s what transformation and an inclusive city requires.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tafelberg, a blue print for cape town and south Africa
metadata.Summary: This is a story of a school that was sold by the Western Cape Government to an organisation without due public process. It raised the ire of organisations because this was the perfect opportunity for local and provincial govt to, in terms of SPLUMA, to redress the imbalances of the past and create affordable housing in the city centre. Something which, contrary to the constitution, the western cape has failed to do since the dawn of democracy. This is the story of how a local NGO got the high court to halt the sale and order a public participation process. At this stage, according to a petition it’s split 50/50, those sea point residents opposed to and for it. We do hone in on a property mogul Seeff properties who took it upon himself to get a petition going not to support the development of this area for affordable housing, and he even took it upon himself to tell the Jewish community not to attend the public process meetings. We hear exactly why adorable housing should be considered in this area of city. One care giver, who was a domestic worker, and who has lived in domestic quarters will describe how and why she should be allowed the opportunity to stay in affordable housing in sea point. She says that people are scared that it will bring the value of properties down in the area but she says "why is it that I downgrade your property if I don’t downgrade your children when you go to work?"
metadata.Further information: In the meantime the public works dept has now issued a report suggesting that affordable housing can be developed in sea point if it is cross subsidized by commercial retail outlets and we will hear from the head of Malcolm McCarthy who heads up the national association of social housing who has travelled extensively overseas and seen how affordable housing can be achieved in cities. We also then show just how the city needs to get its properties right for in the gentrification of the city, some families are being evicted to the landscapes of the cape flats, similar to the evictions which took place during the apartheid era. We will quiz both the city and the province to show us exactly the land that they have which is not being used and which could be used for affordable housing.
